1.pericope_label: And in the second year of the reign of Nebuchadnezzar Nebuchadnezzar dreamed dreams, wherewith his spirit was troubled, and his sleep brake from him. Then the king commanded to call the magicians, and the astrologers, and the sorcerers, and the Chaldeans, for to shew the king his dreams. So they came and stood before the king. And the king said unto them, I have dreamed a dream, and my spirit was troubled to know the dream.

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch derive the four classes of practitioners in turn: the first from the word for a stylus, so men who went about with the pen, learned in the sacred writings; the second from a root meaning to breathe or whisper, since their incantations were worked by movements of the breath; the third the magicians found also in Egypt and, on a prophet's testimony, a powerful body in Babylon; the fourth the Chaldean priestly caste. On the king's demand they deny he had forgotten the dream at all, allowing only an oppressive recollection that he had dreamed, and cite his own later words that if the wise men cannot declare the dream they have agreed to speak deceitfully; they name critics who use the supposed forgetting to call the narrative unhistorical, the demand madness and the rage unmotivated. Ellicott notes the king had been called king of Babylon by anticipation while his father still lived, follows the same derivations for the classes but doubts the last is a separate class at all, taking them for the priests and counting them within the first, observes that the plural dreams gives way at once to the singular since it was one dream of several parts, and holds that the king remembered a portion of the dream while losing its general outline.

Gill surveys the Jewish answers to the chronological difficulty — the second year after the temple fell, the second of the monarchy once the surrounding nations were subdued, the second after the Egyptians were beaten, and a reckoning counted backward from the end of the reign which even Jewish commentators called an unusual way of counting — and rejects them all as too late, since the man was famous for wisdom long before; on the dream itself he holds the king could remember that he had dreamed but not what it was about, and reports a rabbi who claimed the king knew it perfectly and was testing the wise men, which Gill dismisses against the plain words. Calvin prefers the co-regency reckoning, that the king reigned first with his father, and reads the sleeplessness as evidence of the dream's author, since this was not his first dream but the terror impressed on his mind would not let him rest, like a sting keeping him troubled until he had the meaning; he allows that even profane writers rightly connected dreams with divine agency while warning that it would be foolish to extend this to every dream, since dreams also rise from the day's thoughts and men who read a conjecture into each one make themselves ridiculous.

Clarke takes the second year as the fourth by Jewish reckoning, the first two having been shared with the king's father, and reports that nothing remained in the morning but the uneasy impression; he confesses the Chaldeans are hard to identify and guesses at a college where all the arts were professed and taught, the name being kept exclusively by one people among the hundred and twenty provinces. Wesley counts the date as properly the fifth year of the reign but the second after Daniel was brought in, says the magicians assumed the national name as the most noble, treats the plural as one dream of many parts, and holds the king remembered the fact in general without being able to repeat it.

Henry offers two ways round the chronology: that the young man may have been forward enough to be taken into service after one year rather than three, or that the second year is counted from the day he first stood before the king, as an earlier interpreter of dreams rose in the second year after his own skill appeared; he rejects the solution that puts it in the thirty-sixth year of the reign.

debates.question: How is the second year of the reign to be reckoned?

positions.position: By the co-regency, the first two years having been shared with the king's father.
From the day Daniel first stood before the king, whatever year of the reign that was.
None of the late Jewish reckonings will do, since the man was already famous for wisdom.

debates.question: Had the king actually forgotten his dream?

positions.position: Nothing remained in the morning but the uneasy impression.
He remembered it in general but could not repeat it, retaining a portion and losing the outline.
He had not forgotten it at all; only an oppressive recollection remained, and the demand was a test of the wise men's honesty.

outliers.claim: Turns the question of the forgotten dream into a defence of the narrative's historicity, naming critics who used the forgetting to argue that the demand was madness and the king's rage unmotivated.

Grants that even pagan writers were right to connect dreams with divine agency, while warning that reading a portent into every dream is what makes men ridiculous, since dreams also rise from the day's thoughts.

themes: And in the second year of the reign of Nebuchadnezzar Nebuchadnezzar dreamed dreams, wherewith his spirit was troubled, and his sleep brake from him.
Then the king commanded to call the magicians, and the astrologers, and the sorcerers, and the Chaldeans, for to shew the king his dreams. So they came and stood before the king.
And the king said unto them, I have dreamed a dream, and my spirit was troubled to know the dream.

4.pericope_label: Then spake the Chaldeans to the king in Syriack, O king, live for ever: tell thy servants the dream, and we will shew the interpretation. The king answered and said to the Chaldeans, The thing is gone from me: if ye will not make known unto me the dream, with the interpretation thereof, ye shall be cut in pieces, and your houses shall be made a dunghill. But if ye shew the dream, and the interpretation thereof, ye shall receive of me gifts and rewards and great honour: therefore shew me the dream, and the interpretation thereof. They answered again and said, Let the king tell his servants the dream, and we will shew the interpretation of it. The king answered and said, I know of certainty that ye would gain the time, because ye see the thing is gone from me. But if ye will not make known unto me the dream, there is but one decree for you: for ye have prepared lying and corrupt words to speak before me, till the time be changed: therefore tell me the dream, and I shall know that ye can shew me the interpretation thereof. The Chaldeans answered before the king, and said, There is not a man upon the earth that can shew the king’s matter: therefore there is no king, lord, nor ruler, that asked such things at any magician, or astrologer, or Chaldean. And it is a rare thing that the king requireth, and there is none other that can shew it before the king, except the gods, whose dwelling is not with flesh. For this cause the king was angry and very furious, and commanded to destroy all the wise men of Babylon. And the decree went forth that the wise men should be slain; and they sought Daniel and his fellows to be slain.

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch caution that the notice about the language implies nothing about what the king himself spoke; on the phrase the thing is gone from me they set out the case, that two ancient versions treat the word as a verb of departing, which yields that the dream has escaped him, while other interpreters take it otherwise. They say the Chaldeans concealed a confession of ignorance under the claim that the thing was beyond human power, deny that the clause about gods who do not dwell with flesh implies any distinction of higher and lower gods, reading only the plain difference between gods and men with flesh set against spirit as the mark of mortal weakness, and insist the decree was never fully carried out, the participle meaning the killing had merely begun. Ellicott suspects the language notice was a heading telling a copyist where the Aramaic begins, dismisses the conjecture that this portion translates a lost Hebrew original, and supplies his own reason, that what is to be revealed concerns the Gentile world so a Gentile language carries it; he decides the disputed phrase means the order has been published and cannot be recalled, answers that the punishment named was by no means uncommon and points to Assyrian evidence, calls the wise men's appeal to precedent a delicate flattery whose reasoning is that no king ever left a precedent therefore the request is impossible, explains the charge about changing times as an accusation of stalling for a luckier day, finds behind the clause about the gods a Babylonian doctrine in which every man had a deity attached from birth who lived in him and so shared human infirmity, and limits the decree to wise men resident in Babylon.

Gill says the Chaldee runs from this point to the end of the seventh chapter and explains the choice of language as the mother tongue of both parties, easier to speak and to be understood; he notes that some versions read the decree as already executed, and supposes those at court were killed while officers went out for the rest. Calvin allows both senses of the disputed phrase and inclines to the vanished dream, since the expression returns a few verses later where the dream seems meant; he thinks the demand itself unjust, since the wise men professed to interpret dreams and never to recover them, so the king ignores the limits of their art; he observes what all history declares, that the Magi made a trade of their predictions, and sets against them the wise men of the Indies, frugal and austere, who needed neither money nor furniture; and he thinks the wise men's excuse just in itself though the king would not admit it, reading the episode as arranged to prove the Magi impostors.

Clarke agrees the Chaldee runs to the end of the seventh chapter, calls the sentence of dismemberment arbitrary and tyrannical in the extreme while noting providence overruled it to a purpose, and turns the wise men's verdict into evidence, since their own judgment that no man on earth could do it made the young Hebrew's success decisive by their own theology; on the salutation he reaches for a modern parallel, that in the East a superior still blesses an inferior with long life to thee and a poor petitioner uses the same words to a king. Wesley marks the same language change and glosses the classes briefly, the astrologers pretending skill in natural and supernatural things, the sorcerers using diabolical arts, and the Chaldeans assuming a national name.

debates.question: What does the king mean by saying the thing is gone from him?

positions.position: The dream has escaped him; two ancient versions treat the word as a verb of departing.
The order has been published and therefore cannot be recalled.
The versions divide, and the word will bear either construction.

debates.question: What is meant by gods whose dwelling is not with flesh?

positions.position: A Babylonian doctrine of a personal deity attached to each man from birth, dwelling in him and sharing his infirmities; not even those gods could do this.
No distinction of higher and lower gods at all, only the plain difference between gods and men, flesh standing against spirit as the mark of mortal weakness.

outliers.claim: Sets the mercenary Magi against the wise men of the Indies, who were frugal and austere and lived without needing money or furniture at all.
Explains the language change theologically rather than textually: what is about to be revealed concerns the Gentile world, so a Gentile language is made the vehicle of the revelation.

14.pericope_label: Then Daniel answered with counsel and wisdom to Arioch the captain of the king’s guard, which was gone forth to slay the wise men of Babylon: He answered and said to Arioch the king’s captain, Why is the decree so hasty from the king? Then Arioch made the thing known to Daniel. Then Daniel went in, and desired of the king that he would give him time, and that he would shew the king the interpretation. Then Daniel went to his house, and made the thing known to Hananiah, Mishael, and Azariah, his companions: That they would desire mercies of the God of heaven concerning this secret; that Daniel and his fellows should not perish with the rest of the wise men of Babylon.

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch make the captain chief of the bodyguard, the highest office in the kingdom, whose business was to see the king's commands executed, and on the man's name reject a derivation from a Sanskrit word for venerable in favour of a formation from the word for a lion; they render the first verb as answering words of counsel and understanding, correct a rendering that would turn the participle in the question about haste into a predicate and give why is the command so hostile, and note with Ellicott that the title used in the prayer appears once in the patriarchal history but came into common use only during the exile, as the name of the true God set against the gods of the heathen. Ellicott says the question about haste was meant to let the captain understand the thing was not impossible after all, and draws two marks of the man who trusts God rather than his learning: courage, to venture in on a humane errand, and humility, to ask for time, where the wise men had called the thing impossible and never asked an extension; he adds that we are nowhere told the time was granted or that more than an interpretation was promised, many scriptural narratives being very condensed.

Gill offers the guard, the militia, the cooks or the executioners for the captain's office, notes the first verb has been read as inquiring after the law and decree and also as causing the decree to be returned, that is, staying the execution, and prefers the first; he observes that going in was bold on both sides, the captain suspending his orders and Daniel walking into a furious king's presence carrying the name of a wise man, and credits the providence that moved both; he places the house near the palace and rejects a traveller's report setting it twenty miles off, since the orders reached only the wise men of Babylon and Daniel was found among them. Calvin calls the king's failure to send for Daniel sloth, since he should have recalled the incredible gift of heavenly wisdom already seen among the captives of Judah, and adds that God was unwilling his servant should mix with ministers of Satan whose whole knowledge was juggling and error; tyrants are unjust, he says, because they will not undertake the labour of inquiry. He hears an oblique reproach in the question about haste, an expostulation that the man was neither called nor listened to and yet was to die for the failure of others; thinks the prefect was not without fear, being in danger for the delay, and reads it as God bending and taming his mind; and notices that the man who already had the gift, and who alone of the four was a prophet, still calls the other three to implore mercy with him.

Clarke settles the captain's office on the executioners and makes it chief of the butchers, the man who took heads off at the king's displeasure, citing the courtier who fetched a head in a bag on a dish and the officer who carried a prophet's head to a dancing girl, and concluding that with no law, no judge and no jury the king's caprice governs all; he marks the contrast with the Chaldeans, who would not promise so much, pledging only an interpretation if the dream were supplied, while Daniel undertakes to recover the dream as well.

Henry answers the question why the man judged ten times wiser was never sent for by saying that everything was done in a heat and nothing with deliberate thought, but that providence so ordered it, since the magicians being nonplussed first meant the more glory afterwards; meanwhile an undiscriminating sentence condemns him and he knows nothing until notice arrives.

debates.question: What was the captain's office?

positions.position: Chief of the executioners, the butcher who took heads off at the king's pleasure.
Chief of the bodyguard, reckoned the highest office in the kingdom.
Uncertain between the guard, the militia, the cooks and the executioners.

debates.question: Why was Daniel not summoned with the other wise men?

positions.position: Everything was done in a heat, but providence ordered it so that the magicians' failure would come first and the glory afterwards.
The king's sloth, since he should have remembered the gift already seen in the captives; and God did not wish his servant mixed with ministers of Satan.

outliers.claim: Breaks off into a political aside congratulating his countrymen on living under law rather than a prince's caprice, an aside Clarke makes at the same verse in almost the same terms.
Warns that the narrative is very condensed, since we are nowhere actually told that the extension of time was granted or that more than an interpretation had been promised.

themes: Then Daniel answered with counsel and wisdom to Arioch the captain of the king’s guard, which was gone forth to slay the wise men of Babylon:
He answered and said to Arioch the king’s captain, Why is the decree so hasty from the king? Then Arioch made the thing known to Daniel.
Then Daniel went in, and desired of the king that he would give him time, and that he would shew the king the interpretation.
Then Daniel went to his house, and made the thing known to Hananiah, Mishael, and Azariah, his companions:
That they would desire mercies of the God of heaven concerning this secret; that Daniel and his fellows should not perish with the rest of the wise men of Babylon.

19.pericope_label: Then was the secret revealed unto Daniel in a night vision. Then Daniel blessed the God of heaven. Daniel answered and said, Blessed be the name of God for ever and ever: for wisdom and might are his: And he changeth the times and the seasons: he removeth kings, and setteth up kings: he giveth wisdom unto the wise, and knowledge to them that know understanding: He revealeth the deep and secret things: he knoweth what is in the darkness, and the light dwelleth with him. I thank thee, and praise thee, O thou God of my fathers, who hast given me wisdom and might, and hast made known unto me now what we desired of thee: for thou hast now made known unto us the king’s matter.

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch refuse to identify the night vision with a dream: such a vision need not be a dream, Daniel does not call it one, and it is simply a vision received at night while a man is awake; they add that the notion of an identical dream was imported by a critic who wanted a psychological impossibility to discredit the narrative with. On the thanksgiving they note the verb keeps its proper force, the revelation being an address from God and this the answer to it; on the changing of times and seasons they would reverse the Greek order of the two words and distinguish them as the general circumstance of time and the measured point of time, the pairing making the point that all revolutions whatever hang on the will of God. Ellicott agrees it was literally a vision and that a repetition of the king's dream cannot be inferred, finds the doxology built on an existing liturgical form, draws the same contrast between circumstances and epochs of time and ties it to the dream just given, suggests illumination rather than light is the meaning of the last clause since man needs illuminating from a source outside him, and notices that the wisdom acknowledged is not the interpretation but the earlier learning, so the man treats his proficiency in Chaldean studies and his skill with dreams as alike supernatural.

Gill reports the view that the revelation came as a dream, and that Daniel dreamed the king's own dream and remembered what the king forgot, though he leaves open whether the image was shown him sleeping or waking; he runs the range of the changing times from day and night and summer and winter to the revolutions of states, naming the dream's four monarchies, and on the God of the fathers names the patriarchs and the promises made to them. Calvin takes the answered prayer as evidence about the praying, since God showed himself propitious and one driven about like a wave is told he shall receive nothing; he explains the vehemence of the thanksgiving, a man snatched from death beyond expectation being the more stirred to praise, presses the giving of wisdom beyond ordinary prudence to the unusual understanding by which some appear as God's interpreters, which is the gift of prophecy, and uses the phrase about the fathers to set the God of Israel against the multitude of invented deities while guarding it against misuse, since the glory is not founded on ancestral authority as with those who count the ages an error has prevailed and take the consent of mankind for an oracle.

Clarke keeps both options open on the manner of the revelation, that Daniel either dreamed it or had it represented to his mind by immediate inspiration, and says duration and succession are God's, so that because his providence puts down one king and raises another he can tell beforehand what he has purposed for the empires of the earth. Wesley sets the changing of times against the alternatives, that what the heathen ascribed to nature or chance is here ascribed to God, who made all by his power and rules and overrules all by his providence.

debates.question: Did the revelation come as a dream or a waking vision?

positions.position: Possibly a dream, and possibly the very dream the king had dreamed; the text leaves it open whether he was sleeping or waking.
Either a dream or an immediate inspiration; no choice need be made.
A vision and not a dream at all, since a night vision is simply one received while a man is awake.

debates.question: What is meant by changing the times and the seasons?

positions.position: Two distinct words, the general circumstance of time and the measured point of time, jointly asserting that every revolution hangs on God's will.
Everything from day and night and the seasons to the revolutions of states, including the four monarchies of the dream.
A claim against the pagan alternatives, since what the heathen gave to nature or chance is here given to God.

outliers.claim: Reads the closing clause as illumination rather than light, since man needs illuminating from outside himself, and pictures God as a palace in which light dwells.

Guards the appeal to the God of the fathers against the argument from tradition, refusing to found glory on ancestral authority as those do who count up the ages an error has prevailed and treat the consent of mankind as an oracle.

themes: Then was the secret revealed unto Daniel in a night vision. Then Daniel blessed the God of heaven.
Daniel answered and said, Blessed be the name of God for ever and ever: for wisdom and might are his:
And he changeth the times and the seasons: he removeth kings, and setteth up kings: he giveth wisdom unto the wise, and knowledge to them that know understanding:
He revealeth the deep and secret things: he knoweth what is in the darkness, and the light dwelleth with him.

I thank thee, and praise thee, O thou God of my fathers, who hast given me wisdom and might, and hast made known unto me now what we desired of thee: for thou hast now made known unto us the king’s matter.

24.pericope_label: Therefore Daniel went in unto Arioch, whom the king had ordained to destroy the wise men of Babylon: he went and said thus unto him; Destroy not the wise men of Babylon: bring me in before the king, and I will shew unto the king the interpretation. Then Arioch brought in Daniel before the king in haste, and said thus unto him, I have found a man of the captives of Judah, that will make known unto the king the interpretation. The king answered and said to Daniel, whose name was Belteshazzar, Art thou able to make known unto me the dream which I have seen, and the interpretation thereof? Daniel answered in the presence of the king, and said, The secret which the king hath demanded cannot the wise men, the astrologers, the magicians, the soothsayers, shew unto the king; But there is a God in heaven that revealeth secrets, and maketh known to the king Nebuchadnezzar what shall be in the latter days. Thy dream, and the visions of thy head upon thy bed, are these; As for thee, O king, thy thoughts came into thy mind upon thy bed, what should come to pass hereafter: and he that revealeth secrets maketh known to thee what shall come to pass. But as for me, this secret is not revealed to me for any wisdom that I have more than any living, but for their sakes that shall make known the interpretation to the king, and that thou mightest know the thoughts of thy heart.

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch take the parenthesis about the Chaldean name to mean the king knew no Daniel at all, only the name given by the conqueror. Ellicott supposes Babylonian custom allowed only chief officers direct access, as the Persian and Median did, so the earlier approach must also have gone through the captain, and notes it was not strictly true that he had searched for an interpreter though circumstances excuse the language; he reads the parenthesis instead as a reminder to the reader and denies the king was ignorant of the man, having lately examined him, what surprises him being that a novice should succeed where the experienced failed. He says the reply concedes the wise men's case, since what they claimed was true and the gods who dwell with flesh could not reveal this, all power of prediction being denied to heathen gods; takes the word rendered hereafter to mean simply in the course of history and not the Messianic days only; observes that the visions of the head are called thoughts because thinking was the natural channel of a supernatural message, coming unforced while the king's mind was on further conquests; and glosses the disclaimer as meaning not by reason of any wisdom of the speaker's own but for the king's sake.

Gill notes the man went the moment the secret was given though not before giving thanks, and hears in the answer an assertion of one God against the many, revelation belonging to him alone. Calvin raises the objection that magical arts ought rather to be abolished outright, being diabolical, and answers that the corruptions were many but the principles sound, so he would not condemn the whole; he doubts too the interpreters who find magic simply condemned here, and infers from the delay that some Magi were already dead. He agrees the request for time went through the captain, those kings counting courtesy a profanation of their majesty, and adds that the captain's speech shows how courtiers dress up their own good offices; he hears despair in the king's question, the king having thought the Magi alone possessed wisdom, and finds it drawn out of a proud man so the grace should show brighter; and he declines the question of the classes of practitioners, since the Jews themselves can only guess, bold in definition and rash in affirmation while unable to distinguish the sorts.

Clarke has the decree merely suspended pending the trial, notes the last name in the list renders an old English word for tellers of truth but belongs to another class, perhaps men who divined by numbers or amulets, and adds that asking whether the king's own men, aided by his gods, could tell him was necessary so he might see the folly of trusting one and worshipping the other; he says the phrase about the latter days generally means, in the prophets, the Messiah's times. Wesley thinks the king took courage from the name he had bestowed, which means keeper of secret treasure, and admires the approach, that the prophet does not fall abruptly on the dream but prepares a lofty king by degrees, to win him to the true God.

Henry allows some of the wise men deserved death as magicians by God's law but insists what they stood condemned for was no crime worth dying for, so let them live and be justly shamed; since God shows common kindness to evil and good, we should be ready to save even bad men's lives, a good man being a common good, as a ship's company was once given to one prisoner.

debates.question: Should the wise men have been spared at all?

positions.position: Yes; the charge was not a capital crime, and saving even bad men's lives is what common kindness requires.
Yes, though the arts themselves are diabolical; the corruptions were many but the underlying principles sound.
It was simple humanity toward his heathen teachers, and the decree was stopped by that intercession alone.

debates.question: What period does the prophecy speak of?

positions.position: The times of the Messiah, which is what the phrase about the latter days generally means in the prophets.
Simply hereafter, in the course of history, and not the Messianic days only.

outliers.claim: Reads the captain's report of having found a man as an instance of how courtiers dress up their own good offices, since the king had already granted the time through him.
Suggests the king took courage from the Chaldean name he had himself bestowed, since it means keeper of secret treasure.

Then Arioch brought in Daniel before the king in haste, and said thus unto him, I have found a man of the captives of Judah, that will make known unto the king the interpretation.

But there is a God in heaven that revealeth secrets, and maketh known to the king Nebuchadnezzar what shall be in the latter days. Thy dream, and the visions of thy head upon thy bed, are these;
As for thee, O king, thy thoughts came into thy mind upon thy bed, what should come to pass hereafter: and he that revealeth secrets maketh known to thee what shall come to pass.

But as for me, this secret is not revealed to me for any wisdom that I have more than any living, but for their sakes that shall make known the interpretation to the king, and that thou mightest know the thoughts of thy heart.

31.pericope_label: Thou, O king, sawest, and behold a great image. This great image, whose brightness was excellent, stood before thee; and the form thereof was terrible. This image’s head was of fine gold, his breast and his arms of silver, his belly and his thighs of brass, His legs of iron, his feet part of iron and part of clay. Thou sawest till that a stone was cut out without hands, which smote the image upon his feet that were of iron and clay, and brake them to pieces. Then was the iron, the clay, the brass, the silver, and the gold, broken to pieces together, and became like the chaff of the summer threshingfloors; and the wind carried them away, that no place was found for them: and the stone that smote the image became a great mountain, and filled the whole earth.

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch work through the anatomy of the figure, fixing the opening construction as a phrase about the image rather than a sentence, tracing the words for breast, for the belly enclosing the bowels, for the thighs and upper loins, and for the leg including the upper thigh, and noting the clause about the feet is partitive. Ellicott insists on the wording, that it is properly one great image and the oneness is the point: though many members are named, only four parts answer to the four metals, so the history of the world in its bearing on God's people, complicated as it looks, consists of no more than four principal divisions, the further detail given later marking minor complications that do not disturb the fourfold outline. He ends with what the stone did not do, since it never struck the head, breast or loins, which became fragments only by falling once the feet were gone, and adds that the chaff of the summer threshing floors is standing language for divine judgment.

Gill gives the head fine gold for its glory, excellence and duration and takes the iron for a coarser metal that is yet very strong; he alone reads the two legs as the eastern and western empires into which the Roman was later divided. On the stone he takes it for the Messiah and marshals support, that Jewish writers ancient and modern read it so as well as Christians, one old book identifying it with the Shepherd and Stone of Israel and another making the ninth of ten kings the King Messiah; and he says that the basis being broken the whole body came down and shattered by its own weight. Calvin says all writers of sound judgment understand the four monarchies without controversy and charges those who confuse the Turkish empire with the Roman with an ignorance easily proved, since what they are avoiding is the confession that Christ was exhibited to the world; he raises the difficulty that if Christ is the wisdom by whom kings reign his coming should not break up an order God approves, and answers that earthly empires are broken only accidentally, since if kings discharged their office honestly his kingdom would not be against their power, and it is their untameable pride that makes them feel his hand; of the Roman fall he observes that no outside force brought it down, which is why he takes it to have been broken by Christ.

Clarke runs the metals off in order, the head Babylonian, the breast and arms Medo-Persian, the belly and thighs Macedonian, the legs Roman, and the feet that same empire mixed with barbarian nations and divided into ten kingdoms; he calls the stone a fifth monarchy, the spiritual kingdom which lasts for ever and spreads over the whole earth, and distinguishes the kingdom of the stone from that of the mountain.

Henry begins with the transaction, that the king had paid for this man's maintenance and education and preferred him at court and is now repaid, having received a prophet though not in the name of a prophet and so getting a prophet's reward; then he turns the image against its dreamer, since here is a worshipper of images and likely an admirer of statues who had adorned his palace with them, and a great image is now set before him in a dream which might have taught him what the things he spent so much upon really were, seeing he could shut his eyes, represent to himself what forms he pleased and beautify them at will without the expense or trouble of sculpture.

debates.question: What do the two legs signify?

positions.position: The eastern and western empires into which the Roman was later divided.
Simply the Roman empire, the division being marked instead by the feet and toes.

debates.question: How can the stone break kingdoms if God approves civil order?

positions.position: Only accidentally; if kings discharged their office honestly Christ's kingdom would not be against their power, but their pride makes them feel his hand.
The stone is a fifth monarchy of a different kind, spiritual, which outlasts and supersedes all the others.
The stone never struck the upper parts at all; they fell of themselves once the feet were broken.

outliers.claim: Turns the vision against the king's own habit, observing that a man who spent lavishly on statues is shown a great image in a dream, and could have had all the forms he liked by shutting his eyes and saved the cost of sculpture.
Declines the theology of the passage almost entirely in favour of anatomy, working out which Aramaic word covers the belly, the thighs and the upper part of the leg.

themes: Thou, O king, sawest, and behold a great image. This great image, whose brightness was excellent, stood before thee; and the form thereof was terrible.
This image’s head was of fine gold, his breast and his arms of silver, his belly and his thighs of brass,
His legs of iron, his feet part of iron and part of clay.
Thou sawest till that a stone was cut out without hands, which smote the image upon his feet that were of iron and clay, and brake them to pieces.

Then was the iron, the clay, the brass, the silver, and the gold, broken to pieces together, and became like the chaff of the summer threshingfloors; and the wind carried them away, that no place was found for them: and the stone that smote the image became a great mountain, and filled the whole earth.

36.pericope_label: This is the dream; and we will tell the interpretation thereof before the king. Thou, O king, art a king of kings: for the God of heaven hath given thee a kingdom, power, and strength, and glory. And wheresoever the children of men dwell, the beasts of the field and the fowls of the heaven hath he given into thine hand, and hath made thee ruler over them all. Thou art this head of gold. And after thee shall arise another kingdom inferior to thee, and another third kingdom of brass, which shall bear rule over all the earth. And the fourth kingdom shall be strong as iron: forasmuch as iron breaketh in pieces and subdueth all things: and as iron that breaketh all these, shall it break in pieces and bruise. And whereas thou sawest the feet and toes, part of potters’ clay, and part of iron, the kingdom shall be divided; but there shall be in it of the strength of the iron, forasmuch as thou sawest the iron mixed with miry clay. And as the toes of the feet were part of iron, and part of clay, so the kingdom shall be partly strong, and partly broken. And whereas thou sawest iron mixed with miry clay, they shall mingle themselves with the seed of men: but they shall not cleave one to another, even as iron is not mixed with clay.

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch note that only of the third kingdom is it said to rule the whole earth, so in extent and power it surpasses what came before; on the mixture they make iron firmness and clay brittleness and read the mingling as an attempt to bind two materials that will not combine. Ellicott takes the plural in we will tell to include the three companions, to whose intercession the revelation was owed; locates the second kingdom's inferiority in its divided character against the massive solidity of its predecessor, shown by the two breasts answering to the one head as well as by the poorer metal, while granting that in territory and duration it far exceeded the Babylonian; observes that the fourth is treated at much greater length, and that where the second and third each borrowed from the empire before, the Roman crushes out what remains of them and brings in a new system and civilisation; says the outward character remains the strength of iron despite the inward divisions marked by two legs, then two feet, then ten toes, though the strength is only apparent since discordant elements are present which cannot cohere; and takes the mingling with the seed of men for the human attempt at union set against what God will do, marriages arranged between the royal houses of the component kingdoms.

Gill reports Jewish interpreters who join the title king of kings to the next clause and make it a description of God, so that the King of kings who is the God of heaven has given the kingdom, and answers that this runs against the accents; he agrees the second kingdom began as large and as rich, finding the decline in later reigns down to the Darius who lost it; he rules out two candidates for the fourth, not Alexander's successors, who belong to the thighs and in whose time no kingdom of Christ arose, and not the Turkish empire as three Jewish commentators held; and he identifies the ten toes with the kingdoms into which the western empire broke under the northern invasions, the ten horns elsewhere, some strong like iron and lasting, others of clay and short-lived. Calvin explains why the list starts with Babylon, since the Assyrians had been subdued before the monarchy passed there but never prevailed enough to count as supreme, and God was not concerned with what had already happened, the point being that the people should have something to lean on in future while the Chaldeans had sixty or seventy years still to run; he denies the second kingdom inferior in power or wealth, that empire being simply added to the Medo-Persian, and puts the inferiority in the general condition of the world being worse; and he reaches the Roman identification by tracing what became of Alexander's successors, one yielding his kingdom to the free cities, another driven beyond the mountains, Macedonia becoming a province and Egypt being seized.

Clarke keeps the title of the man and presses the giver, since the kingdom came neither from his own gods nor his own prowess, and with it came power to rule, strength to defend and glory for dignity. Wesley reads the plural as piety and modesty, a refusal to arrogate what four had begged from God; gives the reason for the gold as the vast riches of that monarchy and its standing longest, five hundred years, flourishing to the last; makes the second kingdom inferior in time, lasting less than half as long; says brass because coarser, recalling that its king marched to the Indies and was said to have conquered the world; and traces the fourth kingdom's division to civil wars and to provinces throwing off the yoke.

debates.question: In what sense is the second kingdom inferior?

positions.position: In its divided character, set against the massive solidity of its predecessor and shown by two breasts answering to one head.
Not in power or wealth at all, but in the general condition of the world being worse.
In duration, since it lasted less than half as long.
Not at the outset, when it was as large and rich, but in the decline of its later reigns.

debates.question: Should the title king of kings be read of the man or of God?

positions.position: Of the king, whatever Jewish interpreters do with the accents.
Of the king, with the stress falling on the giver of the kingdom rather than the holder.

outliers.claim: Explains the omission of the Assyrians as deliberate: God was not concerned with what had already passed, the point of the prophecy being to give a people still under Chaldean rule something to lean on for the sixty or seventy years remaining.
Reads the mingling with the seed of men as dynastic marriage policy, the human attempt to unite discordant kingdoms set over against what God is about to do.

themes: This is the dream; and we will tell the interpretation thereof before the king.
Thou, O king, art a king of kings: for the God of heaven hath given thee a kingdom, power, and strength, and glory.
And wheresoever the children of men dwell, the beasts of the field and the fowls of the heaven hath he given into thine hand, and hath made thee ruler over them all. Thou art this head of gold.
And after thee shall arise another kingdom inferior to thee, and another third kingdom of brass, which shall bear rule over all the earth.
And the fourth kingdom shall be strong as iron: forasmuch as iron breaketh in pieces and subdueth all things: and as iron that breaketh all these, shall it break in pieces and bruise.

And whereas thou sawest the feet and toes, part of potters’ clay, and part of iron, the kingdom shall be divided; but there shall be in it of the strength of the iron, forasmuch as thou sawest the iron mixed with miry clay.
And as the toes of the feet were part of iron, and part of clay, so the kingdom shall be partly strong, and partly broken.
And whereas thou sawest iron mixed with miry clay, they shall mingle themselves with the seed of men: but they shall not cleave one to another, even as iron is not mixed with clay.

44.pericope_label: And in the days of these kings shall the God of heaven set up a kingdom, which shall never be destroyed: and the kingdom shall not be left to other people, but it shall break in pieces and consume all these kingdoms, and it shall stand for ever.

schools.summary: Ellicott points out that no kings have been mentioned up to this point, so they must be the ones the toes stand for, and takes the sense to be that while the fourth kingdom still contrives to exist in some modified form, its parts at war and in turmoil, the kingdom of God arrives.

Gill will not have any of the first three kingdoms here, nor the old Roman emperors, but only the ten kings of the divided empire; he traces a beginning under Augustus and Tiberius, growth under Constantine, diminution under the Papacy and revival at the Reformation, but holds the kingdom will not be set up in its glory until the ten have been overcome. Calvin spends the verse answering a Jewish commentator who set out six reasons why the fifth kingdom cannot be Christ's. To the objection that since the four kingdoms were earthly the fifth must be of the same nature or the comparison is absurd, he answers that Scripture constantly compares the heavenly kingdom with earthly ones, that no comparison requires every point to match, and that some difference is precisely what should be expected. To the objection that if religion distinguishes kingdoms the first three were all one, since all worshipped idols, he answers that religion was never the distinguishing mark, God having stripped the Babylonians of power and handed the monarchy on in turn. To the objection that this kingdom was to know no passing away though the Turks hold a great part of the world and Christian religion is divided, he answers that the objection assumes what he denies, that the kingdom is visible, since by its nature it is not outward and the saying that this kingdom is not of this world was meant to remove it from the ordinary forms of government. To the objection that the fourth and fifth monarchies would then begin together, he answers that the rabbi has dated the Roman monarchy from Julius Caesar, whereas it began when Macedon was reduced to a province and the third empire started to decline. To the objection that once Constantine professed the faith the empire and the kingdom cannot be separated, he answers that the prophecy ends the Roman empire where it began to be torn in pieces, that tearing being a commonwealth in which all were related and all thought themselves equally kings, a bond which should have made the thing permanent and instead destroyed it.

Clarke stays with the contrast, that every preceding empire was swallowed by the next and this one alone remains to the end of the world, calling it the extensive and extending empire of Christ. Wesley puts the beginning much earlier, while the iron kingdom itself still stood, since the birth fell in the reign of Augustus, and adds that this kingdom is bounded by no limits as worldly empires are but is truly universal.

debates.question: Whose days are the days of these kings?

positions.position: The days of the toes, while the fourth kingdom still exists in some modified form with its parts at war.
While the iron kingdom itself still stood, since the birth fell in the reign of Augustus.
The days of the ten kings of the divided empire; the kingdom began earlier but will not be set up in glory until they are overcome.
At the close of the fourth monarchy, when it began to be torn in pieces.

debates.question: Can the fifth kingdom be Christ's if it is unlike the four?

positions.position: Yes; Scripture constantly compares the heavenly kingdom with earthly ones, and no comparison requires every point to match.
Yes, because it is a kingdom of a different order, spiritual and endless where the others were swallowed one by another.

outliers.claim: Answers a Jewish commentator's objection that the kingdom cannot be Christ's while the Turks hold half the world by denying the premise outright: the kingdom is not visible, and the saying that it is not of this world was meant to remove it from the ordinary forms of government.

Runs a full periodisation through the verse, with the kingdom beginning under Augustus, increasing under Constantine, diminished under the Papacy and revived at the Reformation, its glory still to come.

themes: And in the days of these kings shall the God of heaven set up a kingdom, which shall never be destroyed: and the kingdom shall not be left to other people, but it shall break in pieces and consume all these kingdoms, and it shall stand for ever.

45.pericope_label: Forasmuch as thou sawest that the stone was cut out of the mountain without hands, and that it brake in pieces the iron, the brass, the clay, the silver, and the gold; the great God hath made known to the king what shall come to pass hereafter: and the dream is certain, and the interpretation thereof sure.

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch observe that the mountain went unmentioned when the stone was first described and is used deliberately now, since a stone must be freed from a mountain before it can roll without a hand, and the mountain can only be Zion, where the God of heaven founded the kingdom that spreads from there over the earth; they treat the first half of the verse as confirmation of what had just been said to the king. Ellicott agrees the mountain must be Zion and adds the stone-figure used elsewhere of the Messiah, taking the phrase about hands for the supernatural agency at work; he sets the two objects against each other, the image weak by construction with precious metals at the top and miry clay at the bottom so that the thing was top-heavy, the stone single for all the countless particles composing it and growing in strength as it goes until it becomes a mountain; and he places the present moment before the impact, since the stone is rolling now as the kingdom of God spreads further every day, but the image is still standing and the stone has not yet fallen on it.

Clarke reads the cutting without hands as alluding to the miraculous birth but chiefly to the spiritual nature of a government that used no worldly policy and no military force; in his long discourse on the vision he identifies the legs of iron first with the two kingdoms that came out of Alexander's division, the Egyptian and the Syrian, and only then with the Roman empire which absorbed both, arguing it from the iron's marking not only strength but the violence those houses used against the Jews, and from the marriages arranged between the royal families, which far from binding the kingdoms provoked the bloodiest wars between them. He explains why the gold, silver and brass break along with the iron and clay though only the feet are struck, since the Roman government by then contained the splendour of the Chaldeans, the riches of the Persians, the discipline of the Greeks and the strength of the Egyptian and Syrian houses, with the incoherence of all it had subdued, so that with every political excellence it carried the principles of its own destruction. He separates two kingdoms in the figure, the kingdom of the stone which smites and breaks until no vestige of the others remains, and the kingdom of the mountain which fills what has been subdued and governs it in peace; and he dates the striking, which began when the apostles went out pulling down idolatry and fell decisively at the conversion of Constantine, when the empire happened to be divided among four emperors at once and was thus an epitome of the four monarchies, the stroke being continual in its effects until idolatry is destroyed everywhere. On the closing pair of words he reads a claim about the account itself, that the dream contains a just representation of things as they shall be and its parts have been truly explained. Wesley finds in the stone the small beginning of a visible kingdom and an origin unlike any other, a conception without father or mother according to the two natures, and keeps its double property, grinding to powder what it falls on and growing until it fills the earth.

debates.question: Has the stone already struck the image?

positions.position: Yes; it began striking when the apostles went out and fell decisively at the conversion of Constantine, and the stroke continues in its effects.
No; the stone is rolling and the kingdom spreading, but the image still stands and the blow is future.

debates.question: What do the legs of iron represent?

positions.position: First the Egyptian and Syrian kingdoms of Alexander's successors, and only then the Roman empire that absorbed them both.
A kingdom whose hardness is the point, the interpretation resting on the mountain from which the stone is freed rather than on the legs.

outliers.claim: Notes that at the conversion of Constantine the empire happened to be governed by four emperors at once, and takes that as making it an epitome of the four monarchies at the moment the stone struck it.
Calls the image top-heavy as a matter of construction, precious metals above and miry clay below, and contrasts it with a stone that is single despite the countless particles composing it.

themes: Forasmuch as thou sawest that the stone was cut out of the mountain without hands, and that it brake in pieces the iron, the brass, the clay, the silver, and the gold; the great God hath made known to the king what shall come to pass hereafter: and the dream is certain, and the interpretation thereof sure.

46.pericope_label: Then the king Nebuchadnezzar fell upon his face, and worshipped Daniel, and commanded that they should offer an oblation and sweet odours unto him. The king answered unto Daniel, and said, Of a truth it is, that your God is a God of gods, and a Lord of kings, and a revealer of secrets, seeing thou couldest reveal this secret. Then the king made Daniel a great man, and gave him many great gifts, and made him ruler over the whole province of Babylon, and chief of the governors over all the wise men of Babylon. Then Daniel requested of the king, and he set Shadrach, Meshach, and Abed–nego, over the affairs of the province of Babylon: but Daniel sat in the gate of the king.

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch grant that falling to the earth is used of honour paid to men but the second verb only of divine homage, so that to the king this was a man in whom the gods had manifested themselves, and they set it beside two occasions when an apostle stopped the same thing; they work out the offices conferred and note the word for prefect is a foreign term taken into the language, and they reject a reading that has the man ask to be relieved of his office, since one wishing to keep the dignity and hand over the duty would have needed no appointment, only permission. Ellicott says the word for the worship is always used of adoration offered to an idol and supposes the king thought the gods dwelt in this man more fully than in his other sages; on the confession he gives much less than the others, holding that the king does not acknowledge this God as the true one but only as worthy of a place in the Babylonian pantheon; he admits defeat on the second office conferred, which he says has been inexplicable and awaits further discoveries; and he makes the three friends satraps under Daniel's supervision, reading the gate as marking his higher rank and admission to the inner palace.

Gill argues the worship was religious from the sequel, since the orders that follow rule out civil respect and a proud monarch would never have gone so far for a captive he took to be a mere man, adding that the man was great in spiritual things already and is now made great in worldly ones; he infers from the next verse that the offering was stopped and the king instructed. Calvin alone gives the prostration half a mark, since given the pride of kings, who scarcely reckon themselves among mortals, there was piety and modesty in this one prostrating himself, and the dream cannot have pleased him, having just heard his own flourishing monarchy pronounced short and certain to perish. On the confession he holds both readings at once, that the words are pious and might be taken for proof of real conversion, but profane men are sometimes seized with admiration and will then say everything a true worshipper would, and it lasts no longer than the fit, since they remain wrapped in their superstitions and slip back, as a later episode will show; what he will not give up is the use of it, since God meant a heathen king to herald his own power, which profited the Jews who stayed firm while most of their countrymen turned idolaters in captivity. He warns ministers that where money is not despised many vices spring up and covetous men traffic in the word, though here the gifts were rightly taken; and he raises the suspicion of ambition in the request for the three friends, answering that the motive was pity for his own people, tyrannically used and everywhere hated.

Clarke says flatly that receiving such worship would have been gross idolatry and it must have been forbidden; he counts three gifts in the promotion, the presents, the government of the province and the presidency over the wise men, notes the three friends had shared the danger and helped by their prayers, and observes that the influence reached only the one province, not the empire. Wesley agrees a stop was put to the worship though the prostration and the word of command could not be prevented, takes the confession at full value as naming the supreme God of all the world and notes the word for lord carries the sense of high Lord, and reads the gate as the place where the chief officer waited on the king's business.
Henry has the king treating Daniel as a little god, concluding a divinity was lodged in him.

debates.question: How much credit does the king's prostration deserve?

positions.position: None; receiving such worship would have been gross idolatry, and it must have been forbidden.
Half a mark, since given the pride of kings there was piety and modesty in the act itself.
It was idol-worship by the plain sense of the word, offered to gods the king supposed were dwelling in the man.

debates.question: What does the king's confession amount to?

positions.position: A full acknowledgment of the supreme God of all the world, above every other.
No more than admitting this God to a place in the Babylonian pantheon.
Words pious enough to pass for conversion, but a momentary fit which leaves the man wrapped in his superstitions.

outliers.claim: Raises against the prophet himself the suspicion of ambition in seeking offices for his three friends, and answers it not by denying the advantage but by pleading pity for a people tyrannically used and everywhere hated.
Admits that the second office conferred on Daniel has so far been inexplicable, and leaves it to be cleared up by discoveries not yet made.

themes: Then the king Nebuchadnezzar fell upon his face, and worshipped Daniel, and commanded that they should offer an oblation and sweet odours unto him.
The king answered unto Daniel, and said, Of a truth it is, that your God is a God of gods, and a Lord of kings, and a revealer of secrets, seeing thou couldest reveal this secret.
Then the king made Daniel a great man, and gave him many great gifts, and made him ruler over the whole province of Babylon, and chief of the governors over all the wise men of Babylon.
Then Daniel requested of the king, and he set Shadrach, Meshach, and Abed–nego, over the affairs of the province of Babylon: but Daniel sat in the gate of the king.
